reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank has a cumulative one-year gap (rate-sensitive assets minus rate-sensitive liabilities) of +USD 128m. Rates are expected to fall by 1.5 percentage points over the year.
ask: Net interest income is expected to:

options.label: Rise, by about USD 1.9m
options.why: Sign slip. A positive gap gains when rates rise; a fall in rates squeezes asset income more than funding cost, so NII drops.

options.label: Stay unchanged
options.why: Treated a positive gap as a hedged book. Only a gap near zero leaves NII unaffected by a parallel rate move.

takeaway: Change in NII is about the rate change times the cumulative gap, so a positive gap loses when rates fall.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank has interest-sensitive assets of USD 470m, interest-sensitive liabilities of USD 876m and total assets of USD 1,000m. The dollar gap is already worked out as ISA minus ISL = -USD 406m.
ask: The relative interest-sensitive gap (dollar gap divided by total assets) is closest to:

options.label: About -86%
options.why: Divided the gap by interest-sensitive assets (470) instead of total assets.

options.label: About +41%
options.why: Sign slip: took ISL minus ISA, which flips a liability-sensitive bank into an asset-sensitive one.

options.label: About -0.41%
options.why: Left the ratio $-0.406$ as a decimal and read it as a percent figure.

takeaway: The relative gap scales the dollar gap by total assets, not by either sensitive side; the sign says which side is bigger.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank reports a net interest margin of 2.45%. Interest revenue is USD 100m and interest expense is USD 64m.
ask: Earning assets are closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 4,080m
options.why: Divided interest revenue (100) by the margin instead of net interest income (100 - 64 = 36).

options.label: ≈ USD 14.7m
options.why: Entered the margin as 2.45 instead of 0.0245, a percent-as-decimal slip.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.88m
options.why: Multiplied net interest income by the margin instead of dividing.

takeaway: NIM is net interest income over earning assets; invert it with NII, not revenue, and keep the margin as a decimal.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank has total assets of USD 1,212m and zero equity, so liabilities are also USD 1,212m. Rate-sensitive liabilities are USD 156m and cost 4%. All other liabilities are not rate-sensitive and cost 6%.
ask: Which part of the interest expense bill is larger?

options.label: The non-rate-sensitive liabilities: USD 1,056m at 6%, about USD 63m
The rate-sensitive liabilities: USD 156m at 4%, about USD 6m
options.why: Treated the USD 156m as the whole liability side. With zero equity the other 1,056 is also funded, at 6%.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The 6% rate is only 1.5 times the 4% rate, but the base is nearly seven times larger, so the non-rate-sensitive leg dominates.

takeaway: With zero equity every asset is funded by a liability; the big non-rate-sensitive block drives the interest bill.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank has interest-sensitive assets of USD 500m and interest-sensitive liabilities of USD 300m.
ask: The interest-sensitivity ratio, ISA / ISL, is:

options.label: Above 1, so the bank is asset sensitive
Below 1, so the bank is liability sensitive
options.why: Inverted the ratio: ISL / ISA = 0.60 is the reciprocal, not the interest-sensitivity ratio.

options.label: Exactly 1
options.why: The ratio is 1 only when ISA equals ISL; here assets exceed liabilities by USD 200m.

takeaway: ISA over ISL above 1 means more assets than liabilities reprice: asset sensitive, positive gap.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: ABC Bank reports: interest income USD 143m, interest expense USD 128m, total earning assets USD 950m, shareholders equity USD 300m, cash USD 93m.
ask: Net interest margin (net interest income over earning assets) falls in which range?

options.label: Between 2% and 10%
options.why: Divided net interest income by equity (15 / 300 = 5.0%) instead of earning assets.

options.label: Above 10%
options.why: Used gross interest income, not net: 143 / 950 = 15.1%. The margin is on the spread over funding cost.

takeaway: NIM is a thin number: net interest income is a small residual of two large flows, divided by earning assets.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank has assets of USD 180m with duration 4 years and liabilities of USD 150m with duration 3 years. Market yields jump from 9% to 13%.
ask: Using duration, the bank's net worth:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Looked only at the liability side: liabilities lose about USD 16.5m, which looks like a gain. Assets lose more, about USD 26.4m.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Assumed both sides moving cancels out. Dollar durations are 720 (assets) against 450 (liabilities), so they do not offset.

takeaway: Net worth moves by the change in assets minus the change in liabilities; the longer, larger asset side loses more when yields rise.

reading: LTR-1: Liquidity Risk
setup: Liquidity-adjusted VaR = regular VaR + cost of unwinding in a normal market. One-day 99% VaR is GBP 9.4m. Equity block: mid value GBP 200m, quote bid 49.80 / offer 50.20. Corporate bond: mid value GBP 150m, quote bid 98.70 / offer 99.30.
ask: The cost of unwinding (the add-on to VaR) is closest to:

options.label: GBP 2.5m
options.why: Charged the full bid-offer spread on each position instead of half. Selling crosses only half the spread, from mid to bid.

options.label: GBP 10.65m
options.why: That is the full liquidity-adjusted VaR (9.4 + 1.25), not the add-on itself.

takeaway: Unwinding costs half the proportional spread times mid value; the add-on is small next to the VaR itself.

reading: LTR-1: Liquidity Risk
setup: Stressed liquidity-adjusted VaR, spreads normal, 99% spread confidence ($\lambda = 2.326$). Provincial bonds: mid value CAD 120m, proportional spread mean 1.0%, sd 1.2%. A stock position of 2m shares quoted bid CAD 39.60 / offer CAD 40.40, with dollar spread mean CAD 0.16 and sd CAD 0.20. Regular VaR is CAD 7.5m.
ask: The stressed cost of liquidation (the add-on to the VaR) is closest to:

options.label: ≈ CAD 0.76m
options.why: Used mean spreads only and dropped the $\lambda\sigma$ term, which gives the normal-market cost.

options.label: ≈ CAD 27m
options.why: Fed the stock's dollar spread (0.16, 0.20) in as proportions instead of dividing by the CAD 40 mid.

options.label: ≈ CAD 0.29m
options.why: Scale slip (1/10×): stressed spreads are several times the mean, so the cost cannot be below the normal-market 0.76.

takeaway: Stressed cost uses mean plus lambda times sd per position, with dollar spreads converted to proportions first.

reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: A fund holds 2m shares quoted bid SGD 25.10 / ask SGD 25.30. Daily changes in the relative spread are normal with zero mean and volatility 0.45%. The 99% transaction cost uses the spread risk factor $\tfrac12(\bar s + 2.33\sigma_s)$ times position value.
ask: The 99% spread risk factor is closest to:

options.why: Dropped the $2.33\sigma_s$ term, leaving only the expected half-spread $\tfrac12\bar s$.
Dropped the current spread $\bar s$ and kept only $\tfrac12(2.33\sigma_s)$.
Forgot the factor $\tfrac12$ in front of the bracket.

takeaway: The 99% spread factor adds 2.33 volatilities to the current relative spread, then takes half because selling crosses half the spread.

reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: A fund holds 2.4m shares of a stock that trades about 1.2m shares a day. Its policy caps its own selling at 25% of daily volume, and it liquidates in equal parts at each day end.
ask: The time to escape the position is closest to:

options.label: 2 trading days
options.why: Ignored the 25% cap and assumed the fund can sell the whole 1.2m shares of daily volume.

options.label: 0.5 trading days
options.why: Multiplied by the 25% cap instead of letting it limit the daily sale: 2.4 / 1.2 × 0.25.

takeaway: Time to escape is the position over the shares the fund will actually trade each day, not over total market volume.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: A thrift uses the structure-of-funds approach and wants to meet all good loan demand at 100%. Loans are USD 117m today but recently peaked at USD 132m, and loans are expected to grow 8% a year. Loan potential is the recent peak grown at the trend rate.
ask: The extra loan liquidity requirement above today's loans is closest to:

options.label: USD 15m
options.why: Used the recent peak without growing it: 132 - 117.

options.label: USD 9.4m
options.why: Grew today's 117 by 8% instead of the recent peak: 117 × 1.08 - 117.

options.label: USD 143m
options.why: Stopped at potential loans (132 × 1.08) and did not subtract the loans already on the books.

takeaway: The loan requirement is potential loans minus current loans; potential loans start from the recent peak.

reading: LTR-7: Monitoring Liquidity
setup: A bank builds its term structure of expected cash flows (CAD m). Assets earn 5% and liabilities cost 3%, paid each year end on balances outstanding that year; an item pays interest in its maturity year. Items: bonds held 60 (mature year 1), loans 140 (year 4), deposits 50 (year 2), bonds issued 110 (year 5), equity 40 (repaid only at end of business). No initial cash.
ask: After year 2, the cumulated expected cash flow is:

options.label: Negative, about CAD -48m
options.why: Took the year-2 flow alone (7.0 - 50 - 4.8 = -47.8) and forgot to cumulate year 1's inflow of 65.2.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Assumed the 60 bond redemption just pays for the 50 deposits. Year-1 net interest and the surplus of 10 still leave a positive balance.

takeaway: Cumulate the flows: a big year-2 outflow does not turn the cumulated position negative if year 1 left a larger inflow.

reading: LTR-7: Monitoring Liquidity
setup: A French bank has initial cash of EUR 1.5m and expected cash flows for years 1 to 6 of +15.0, -6.0, +2.0, -16.5, +1.2, -0.9 (EUR m).
ask: The lowest point of the cumulated position (including initial cash) is:

options.label: -5.5, at year 4
options.why: Left out the initial cash of 1.5 when cumulating.

options.label: -16.5, at year 4
options.why: Read the year-4 single-year flow as the position, without cumulating the earlier surplus.

options.label: -3.7, at year 6
options.why: Assumed the last date is the worst. Years 5 and 6 recover and then slip back, but stay above year 4.

takeaway: The binding date is the minimum of the running total, which starts from initial cash.

reading: LTR-7: Monitoring Liquidity
setup: A bank repos EUR 800,000 notional of an 8% annual-coupon bond (semiannual) three months after a coupon date. The expected clean price is 99.60, accrued interest is 2% of notional, the haircut is 12%. The clean value of the repoed notional is EUR 796,800.
ask: The cash raised at the start of the repo is:

options.label: Lower than EUR 796,800: the 12% haircut outweighs the 2% accrued interest
Higher than EUR 796,800: accrued interest is added on top
options.why: Added the accrued interest (dirty value EUR 812,800) and stopped before applying the haircut.

options.label: About equal to EUR 796,800
options.why: Assumed the haircut and the accrued interest cancel. The haircut cuts 12% of value; accrued adds only 2%.

takeaway: A repo lends the dirty value less the haircut, so a large haircut can leave the cash below even the clean value.

reading: LTR-7: Monitoring Liquidity
setup: A bank holds AUD 2m notional of a 6% annual-coupon bond paying semiannually. Three months after a coupon date it enters a six-month sell/buyback on AUD 800,000 notional. Coupons paid before the buyback belong to the buyer. The full holding would pay a coupon of AUD 60,000 on the next coupon date.
ask: The coupon the bank records in its expected cash flows on that date is:

options.label: Lower than AUD 60,000: AUD 36,000 on the AUD 1.2m still owned
AUD 60,000, unchanged
options.why: That is the repo treatment, where the bank keeps ownership and every coupon. In a sell/buyback the buyer owns the bond.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Only the 800,000 sold passes to the buyer; the bank still owns and is paid on the remaining 1.2m.

takeaway: In a sell/buyback ownership passes, so the coupon on the sold notional leaves the seller's cash flows; in a repo it does not.

reading: LTR-7: Monitoring Liquidity
setup: A bank has initial cash of SGD 2.0m and expected cash flows (SGD m) for years 1 to 6 of +3.0, -4.5, -6.0, +1.0, -1.5, +45.0, including 5% year-end coupons on 40 notional of a bond. It sells part of the bond at the end of year 3, just after the coupon, at 98.00. The lowest cumulated position before any sale is -6.0, at year 5. The naive sale to cover it is 6.0 / 0.98 = 6.12.
ask: The true minimum notional to sell is:

options.label: Higher than 6.12: the coupons given up deepen the deficit in years 4 and 5
Lower than 6.12
options.why: Counted the cash from the sale but not the 5% coupons given up in years 4 and 5, then thought a smaller sale is enough.

options.label: Exactly 6.12
options.why: Covered the year-5 deficit at the sale price but ignored that each unit sold also removes a 5% coupon in years 4 and 5.

takeaway: Selling a coupon bond early costs its later coupons, so the amount needed is more than deficit divided by price.

reading: LTR-12: Managing Non-Deposit Liabilities
setup: A bank raises GBP 500m of new funds (deposits, interbank borrowing and equity). The expected interest and operating costs on all of them total GBP 38.0m, which is 7.60% of the money raised. Only part of each source can be placed in earning assets, between 50% and 95%, GBP 387m in total.
ask: The minimum before-tax return the bank must earn on new earning assets to cover these costs is:

options.label: Below 7.60%
options.why: Divided the costs by a larger base. The base is the money placed in earning assets, which is smaller than the money raised.

options.label: Exactly 7.60%
options.why: Assumed every pound raised is invested. Reserves and other non-earning uses take about a quarter of the funds.

takeaway: The hurdle rate spreads the cost of all new funds over only the part that earns, so it exceeds the cost per pound raised.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: Repricing schedule over one year, USD m, assets / liabilities that are interest sensitive: next 7 days 60 / 45; 8 to 30 days 140 / 190; 31 to 90 days 95 / 120; 91 to 360 days 210 / 225.
ask: The one-year cumulative gap (ISA minus ISL, all buckets) is closest to:

options.label: +USD 15m
options.why: Took only the first bucket, which is asset sensitive, and stopped there.

options.label: +USD 75m
options.why: Sign slip: subtracted assets from liabilities.

options.label: -USD 50m
options.why: Took the largest single bucket (8 to 30 days) instead of the sum of all four.

takeaway: Cumulate every bucket inside the horizon; the early asset-sensitive bucket is outweighed by the liability-sensitive ones.

reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
setup: A bank has assets of JPY 600bn with average duration 2.8 years and liabilities of JPY 540bn. It wants net worth immune to small parallel rate changes.
ask: Compared with the asset duration of 2.8 years, the liability duration it needs is:

options.label: The same, 2.8 years
options.why: Matched durations ignoring leverage. The smaller liability base must have a longer duration to offset the same yen change in value.

options.label: Shorter, about 2.5 years
options.why: Scaled by liabilities over assets instead of assets over liabilities: 2.8 × 540/600 = 2.52.

takeaway: Immunisation matches dollar durations, so when liabilities are smaller than assets their duration must be longer.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A bond has a USD 1,000 face value, a 6% annual coupon, 10 years to maturity and a yield to maturity of 5%.
ask: Its Macaulay duration is:

options.label: Equal to 10 years
options.why: Duration equals maturity only for a zero-coupon bond; coupons return part of the value early.

options.label: Above 10 years
options.why: Duration is a weighted average of payment times, none later than year 10, so it cannot exceed maturity.

takeaway: Coupons pull the average payment time forward, so duration of a coupon bond is shorter than its maturity.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A 20-year bond pays a 7% annual coupon on USD 1,000 face value. The yield to maturity is 10%.
ask: As a step in finding its duration, the bond's price is closest to:

options.label: About USD 1,000, at par
options.why: A bond prices at par only when the coupon equals the yield; here 7% is below 10%.

options.label: About USD 1,255, above par
options.why: Reversed the price-yield relation: a coupon below the yield means a discount, not a premium.

takeaway: Coupon below yield means price below par; sanity-check the price before computing the weighted times.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A bond has a duration of 8.89 years. Yields on comparable bonds fall from 7.50% to 7.25%.
ask: The approximate percentage change in the bond's price is closest to:

options.why: Left out the duration and used only $\Delta y/(1+y)$.
Read the 0.25-point fall as 2.5 points, a factor-of-ten slip.
Used the new yield level 7.25% instead of the 0.25-point change in yield.

takeaway: Use the change in yield, not its level, scale by duration and by 1 + y, and the sign is opposite to the yield move.

reading: LTR-7: Monitoring Liquidity
setup: Base case: deposit withdrawals of USD 25m a month and 30% drawdown on USD 120m of committed credit lines over the year. Stress case: withdrawals USD 35m a month and drawdown of 55%.
ask: Which change adds more outflow over the 12 months?

options.label: The extra credit-line drawdown, +USD 30m
options.why: Compared a 25-point jump with a USD 10m monthly step without annualising or applying it to the USD 120m base: 0.25 × 120 = 30 against 10 × 12 = 120.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Both look like moderate increases, but one is a monthly amount repeated 12 times.

takeaway: Annualise monthly flows before comparing; percentage drawdowns apply to the committed amount, not to a monthly figure.

reading: LTR-9: Liquidity Stress Testing
setup: A bank has a normal liquidity asset buffer of USD 60.0m. Under stress, outflows are USD 28.0m and inflows are USD 15.0m. It also holds USD 16.0m of operational liquidity, which runs day-to-day payments and cannot meet general liabilities.
ask: The net stressed drain on the buffer is closest to:

options.label: USD 43m
options.why: Added inflows to outflows (28 + 15) instead of netting them.

options.label: USD 28m
options.why: Used outflows alone and ignored the inflows that offset them.

options.label: USD -3m
options.why: Also deducted the USD 16m operational liquidity. It is neither added nor subtracted.

takeaway: The stressed buffer is the normal buffer less outflows plus inflows; operational liquidity stays out of it.
